modules.title: Introduction & Foundations
modules.content: A full stack developer works across the entire application — the front end (what users see and interact with in the browser) and the back end (the server, business logic, and database). When you visit a website, your browser sends an HTTP request to a server; the server processes it, often reading or writing to a database, and sends back a response — usually HTML, or JSON for dynamic apps. In this course you'll build both sides: structuring pages with HTML, styling them with CSS, adding interactivity with JavaScript, and eventually connecting a page to a backend that stores real data.

modules.title: Core Skills Walkthrough
modules.content: This module's video is a placeholder sample clip standing in for a recorded lesson — swap it for your own screen-recorded walkthrough. In a real version of this lesson, you would watch a live build of a simple page: writing semantic HTML for a layout, applying CSS for spacing and color, and using JavaScript to respond to a button click and update the page without reloading it.

modules.title: Hands-on Project & Best Practices
modules.content: Now put the pieces together conceptually: a form on the front end collects user input and sends it to a backend route; the backend validates the data, saves it, and returns a JSON response; the front end reads that response and updates the page. Good habits to build early: keep your front-end and back-end code in separate, clearly named folders; never hardcode secrets — use environment variables; and commit your work often with Git so you always have a history to fall back on.

modules.title: Introduction & Foundations
modules.content: Data science is the process of turning raw data into insight. The typical pipeline looks like: collect data, clean it (handle missing or messy values), explore it visually, build a model, and communicate the results. Python is the most common language for this work, largely thanks to libraries like pandas (for tabular data), numpy (for numeric computation), and matplotlib (for visualization).

modules.title: Core Skills Walkthrough
modules.content: This module's video is a placeholder sample clip standing in for a recorded lesson. A real lesson here would walk through loading a CSV into a dataframe, spotting and handling missing values, and producing a first chart — a histogram or scatter plot — to understand the shape of the data before modeling anything.

modules.title: Hands-on Project & Best Practices
modules.content: Once your data is clean, you can start modeling. Regression predicts a continuous number (like a price), while classification predicts a category (like spam vs. not spam). A critical practice is splitting your data into a training set and a test set — you fit the model on the training set and evaluate it on data it has never seen, which is how you catch overfitting: a model that memorizes training data but fails to generalize.

modules.title: Introduction & Foundations
modules.content: UX (user experience) design is about how a product feels and functions for the person using it — is it easy to understand, efficient, and satisfying? UI (user interface) design is the visual layer: colors, typography, spacing, and components. Good design starts with user-centered research: talking to real users, understanding their goals, and identifying pain points before drawing a single screen.

modules.title: Core Skills Walkthrough
modules.content: This module's video is a placeholder sample clip standing in for a recorded lesson. A real lesson here would demonstrate sketching a low-fidelity wireframe for a screen, then turning it into an interactive prototype where buttons and links can be clicked to simulate the real flow before any code is written.

modules.title: Hands-on Project & Best Practices
modules.content: Once a prototype exists, test it with real users and watch where they get confused. Apply usability heuristics — clear feedback, consistency, error prevention — and accessibility basics like sufficient color contrast and descriptive alt text for images. Design is iterative: expect to revise a screen multiple times based on feedback rather than getting it perfect on the first try.

modules.title: Introduction & Foundations
modules.content: Security is often summarized by the CIA triad: Confidentiality (only authorized people can see data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), and Availability (systems stay up and usable). Threats come in many forms — from social engineering that targets people, to malware that targets systems — and defending against them starts with understanding what you're protecting and why it matters.

modules.title: Core Skills Walkthrough
modules.content: This module's video is a placeholder sample clip standing in for a recorded lesson. A real lesson here would cover, at a conceptual and defensive level, how phishing emails try to look legitimate to trick a person into revealing credentials, and how malware can spread — framed entirely around recognition and prevention, not how to create either.

modules.title: Hands-on Project & Best Practices
modules.content: Strong defensive habits go a long way: use unique, strong passwords with a password manager; enable multi-factor authentication wherever it's offered; keep software patched, since updates frequently fix known vulnerabilities; and follow the principle of least privilege — give every account only the access it actually needs, nothing more.

modules.title: Introduction & Foundations
modules.content: Cloud computing delivers computing resources — servers, storage, databases — over the internet instead of on local hardware. Service models range from IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service, like renting a virtual machine) to PaaS (Platform as a Service, where the platform manages the OS/runtime for you) to SaaS (Software as a Service, like a ready-to-use web app). Deployment models include public, private, and hybrid clouds.

modules.title: Core Skills Walkthrough
modules.content: This module's video is a placeholder sample clip standing in for a recorded lesson. A real lesson here would walk through deploying a simple web app to a cloud platform conceptually: packaging the app, choosing a compute option, and pointing a domain at the deployed service.

modules.title: Hands-on Project & Best Practices
modules.content: Two ideas define cloud economics: scalability (the ability to handle more load by adding resources) and elasticity (automatically scaling resources up or down as demand changes, so you're not paying for idle capacity). Combined with pay-as-you-go pricing, this is why cloud computing is attractive compared to buying and maintaining physical servers.

modules.title: Introduction & Foundations
modules.content: Artificial Intelligence is the broad idea of machines performing tasks that typically require human intelligence. Machine Learning (ML) is a subset of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed with rules. Deep Learning is a subset of ML that uses neural networks with many layers, and it powers many modern applications like image recognition and language models.

modules.title: Core Skills Walkthrough
modules.content: This module's video is a placeholder sample clip standing in for a recorded lesson. A real lesson here would visually explain, at a conceptual level, how a neural network takes an input, passes it through layers of weighted connections, and adjusts those weights over many examples to gradually improve its predictions.

modules.title: Hands-on Project & Best Practices
modules.content: AI systems are only as good as the data they learn from — if training data reflects unfair or unbalanced patterns, the model can learn and amplify that bias. Responsible AI development means actively considering fairness, transparency (can you explain why the model made a decision?), and accountability, not just raw accuracy.
